payload.text: Asia’s startup funding held up at the second-highest level in years in the third quarter, even as investment fell slightly from Q2 totals. Overall, investors put $38.5 billion into reported seed- through growth-stage financings for countries in the region in Q3, per Crunchbase data. Of that, a majority went to AI-focused companies, echoing the trends we’ve seen globally . Deal counts, meanwhile, were relatively flat. That indicates concentration of capital into favored startups remains pronounced but is not intensifying. Table of contents An AI-driven quarter China leads by far in country-by-country breakdown Late stage Early stage Seed A big quarter for China Methodology Glossary of funding terms An AI-driven quarter Around 55% of investment — an estimated $21 billion — went to AI-focused companies. Total funding is down substantially from the prior quarter, which was boosted by a $7.4 billion financing for China’s DeepSeek , but still the second-highest tally on record. For Q3, a couple of extra-large rounds bolstered the AI investment tally. The largest went to Beijing-based foundational model company Moonshot AI , which secured $3.5 billion in July at a reported $35 billion valuation. Kling AI , the AI spinout of China-based short video platform Kuaishou Technology , was the second-biggest fundraiser. The generative video startup raised around $3 billion in a July financing that included Baidu and Tencent . China leads by far in country-by-country breakdown China was the leading Asian destination for venture investment by a very wide margin. Per Crunchbase data, roughly $27 billion — or 70% of all Asian startup funding in Q3 — went to China-based companies. India was a distant second, with $2.9 billion, followed by Singapore, with $2.5 billion. For perspective, below we charted third-quarter startup funding tallies for the six countries with the largest totals. Late stage Most capital went to late- and growth-stage funding rounds. Per Crunchbase data, investment at this stage totaled around $20 billion in Q3. That’s down a bit from the prior quarter but nearly double year-ago levels and the second-strongest showing in four years. Multiple jumbo rounds kept the total high. The largest was Moonshot AI’s aforementioned $3.5 billion Series F. Several others raised financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. Shenzhen-based D-Robotics , a provider of robotics hardware and software, for instance, picked up $400 million in a September Series C. And Hong Kong-based Qupital , an e-commerce fintech platform, secured $300 million in Series C funding as it eyes an IPO. Early stage Early-stage investment drifted lower in Q3 but remained at historically high levels. Per Crunchbase data, financing for startups at the Series A and Series B stages totaled $13.6 billion for the just-ended quarter. That’s a decline of 28% from the prior quarter but up 65% from year-ago levels. Seed Reported seed funding hit its highest level in years, boosted by investor enthusiasm around AI. In total, investors poured $4.9 billion into reported seed and angel deals across Asia, per Crunchbase data. That’s up around 22% from the prior quarter and more than double year-ago levels. A big quarter for China Overall, Q3 was a robust period for venture funding to China-based companies, with far smaller sums going to other Asian startup hubs. Funding to startups based in India and Singapore was down significantly quarter over quarter, while Israel’s investment totals declined slightly. We’ll keep an eye out in the coming months to see if this divergence of fortunes persists. payload.text: By Eric Francia How would you handle a junior employee questioning the way you’ve always done something? Might you roll your eyes and dismiss their comments as naivety? Or would you indulge their curiosity? As AI has made knowledge accessible on a scale never seen before, companies are becoming leaner and operating faster. What once took a large team months to do can now be done by a handful of people in a few days. It is undeniable that autonomous systems are changing the way we work. In the small and dynamic teams of the future, choosing the right humans to direct your AI systems will become make or break for a company. As a six-time founder, I’ve learned the best workplaces are the ones where questioning things is the norm. Here’s how to build a team that questions orders as much as it obeys them. AI by design Eric Francia, co-founder and CEO of Uniplay. “AI by design” doesn’t only mean building the right autonomous systems. It’s also about creating autonomous humans. You need to trust the human in the loop as much as you do the technology. The team around you ultimately shapes the company in ways you can’t control. So surrounding yourself with people you trust to make decisions when you’re not in the room is critical to success. The nature of job roles is changing. A job description can be totally different from the one advertised by the time you’ve found a candidate, and a six-month roadmap is outdated by the time you’ve finished drawing it up. The World Economic Forum has stated that 59% of employees will need to reskill by 2030 as AI reshapes the workplace. Hiring for a fixed set of skills won’t move the needle. The people worth investing in are those who are able to learn what comes next. Hire for curiosity Curiosity is the best trait you can hire for. When I look at a CV, it’s not just experience or academic credentials that draw me in. I look for what people have built on the side. What have they made on their own initiative? Hire for curiosity, and you’ll create an environment where people are willing to throw new ideas around and challenge outdated ways of doing things. If your team is worried about saying the wrong thing, they won’t end up saying the right thing either. In a world where technology is turning everything on its head, the companies that will thrive are the ones with curious people who are able to adapt to change quickly. Hand over real responsibility Employees with autonomy operate faster. They make better decisions because company vision is not abstract to people who are given real responsibility to drive it. Being involved in strategic direction stitches an employee into the fabric of the company and keeps them engaged. Trust your employees to know what isn’t working. Allow people to pursue new ideas and reinvent things. Your employees are likely to spot potential problems before you do when they’re closer to the product. Make sure your team has the autonomy to try to fix them before they take hold. Boredom is a big business risk As companies become smaller, employee retention is more important than ever. Losing your best people is costlier when you have fewer of them to begin with. The effects of a bored employee surface quickly in a small team. Boredom makes talented people a little bit slower, and a lot less likely to try the difficult thing. The challenge for modern leaders is keeping your team engaged and interested. A bored employee is more likely to be swayed by a flattering LinkedIn recruiter. Make sure to invest in development, keep your team learning, and always encourage curiosity. Give people autonomy and responsibility from the beginning, and boredom has nowhere to take hold. The mentality of risk and the drive to challenge something outdated is what you need to succeed in the changing work environment. Dare to be a beginner, and teach your team to do the same. That junior employee questioning how you’ve always done things could be the most valuable person in the room. Eric Francia is co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Uniplay , an agent-driven, game-based learning platform. He has experience building, exiting and scaling digital companies across 70 countries. Uniplay is his sixth company to date. Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: It’s an insecure world out there, and investors are responding by scaling up their cybersecurity spending. For the third quarter of 2026, global cybersecurity- and privacy-focused startups pulled in a total of $6.8 billion, per Crunchbase data. That’s up about 50% from the prior quarter and tied for the highest quarterly tally in years, as charted below. The funding bump was due to larger rounds, not more of them. Round counts actually declined sequentially across all stages last quarter, Crunchbase data shows. Biggest cybersecurity fundraisers AI startups accounted for the overwhelming majority of cybersecurity funding, with a particular focus on identity security. Overall, at least 18 companies at the intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity closed rounds of $100 million or more this past quarter. Of those, the largest funding recipient by far was enterprise identity security provider Keyfactor , which picked up $1 billion in a July growth round led by Summit Partners . Founded in 2001, the Ohio company isn’t exactly a startup, but it has attracted the bulk of its venture funding in the past 10 years and its pivot to AI is also of a more recent vintage. Dallas-based Island tied for second place with a $400 million September Series F led by Evolution Equity Partners . The startup, which offers tools for enterprises to see and govern how people and AI agents interact with applications and data, also secured a post-money valuation of $6.4 billion. Cyera , operator of an enterprise data security platform focused on AI agents, also announced a fresh $400 million Goldman Sachs Growth Equity -led investment in September, just three months after raising $600 million. The latest infusion set a $12 billion valuation for the New York startup. For a bigger-picture view of leading fundraisers, below we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 largest round recipients. Exits, too We also saw some good-sized acquisitions of cybersecurity startups this past quarter, even as the IPO market was fairly sluggish. Visa led the M&A pack with its $2.4 billion purchase of anti-fraud technology provider BioCatch in August. The acquisition is part of a broader effort by Visa to beef up its fraud detection and prevention capabilities for the AI age. Among private unicorns, meanwhile, Cyera proved it can find a way to spend a good chunk of the capital it raised. It acquired Oasis Security , an enterprise access management platform built for AI agents, in a deal reportedly valued around $1 billion. As for public offerings, Aura , which offers digital security services to consumers, was the lone sizable venture-backed market debut. The Boston-based startup completed an acquisition of an Australian public company, Qoria , in July, and then renamed the combined company Aura. Overall, an upbeat quarter Overall, Crunchbase funding data points to an upbeat environment for cybersecurity startup funding. This doesn’t seem particularly surprising given the steady drumbeat of worrisome news about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI technology. It’s not an especially reassuring time for most of us. But for cybersecurity founders, there’s certainly an ever-expanding array of hazards to keep at bay. We’ll keep watching in the current quarter to see if investment momentum continues to build. payload.text: While helping another founder build an app that collected information about class-action settlements, Zim Hang came to learn how challenging it can be for consumers to seek compensation from companies they believe wronged them. He also discovered mass arbitration, a way to pursue individual claims when companies’ contracts prevent customers from joining class actions. At the same time, he also realized that relatively few law firms were set up to manage thousands of those claims at once. Zim Hang, founder and CEO of Chariot Claims. (Courtesy photo) That gap became the basis for Chariot Claims , which has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Silverton Partners to help consumers pursue claims over alleged privacy violations, hidden fees and subscriptions that are difficult to cancel. Indicator Ventures , Lightbank , Neon Fund , ZVC , Rosecliff Ventures , Alumni Ventures , FJ Labs , Graph Ventures and Vermilion Ventures also participated in the financing. The New York-based startup works with law firms to identify potential cases, find affected consumers and gather information needed to pursue compensation. The round brings its total funding to $15.7 million, which includes a $3.6 million seed investment in April 2025 and an earlier pre-seed round. Chariot’s latest round comes amid a surge in investment across legal tech. Funding to the legal tech space hit a record high last year, with $4.6 billion invested, per Crunchbase data . So far this year, legal tech startups have pulled in more than $3 billion, putting the sector on pace to match or exceed the 2025 total. The Chariot process works like this: For each case, consumers complete an intake questionnaire that assesses preliminary eligibility in real time. Chariot’s team then reviews these pre-qualified claims through a multi-layered system of technology and human oversight before sending it to the partner law firm handling the case. Hang, the company’s CEO, told Crunchbase News that Chariot typically receives more than 200,000 claim submissions per month and that it has taken on roughly 80 cases since shifting to its current business model just over a year ago. The company has about 15 employees and is currently breaking even, he said. It plans to spend the new funding primarily on hiring and product development, including AI tools to review cases and help determine whether consumers qualify to participate. A gap in consumer legal services Chariot is Hang’s third startup. His first company grew out of sleep research he conducted while studying psychology and neuroscience at Washington University . He turned that research into a smart-pillow business and later sold its intellectual property to a medical-device operator. He later worked in healthcare technology and fintech, founded a startup in the Web3 space, and then moved into legal technology. Across those industries, he said, he encountered complicated systems in which the interests of businesses and their customers did not always align. His experience helping the class-action settlement startup brought those concerns into focus. He described being “frustrated and mystified and horrified by how our justice system works.” Chariot started about three years ago, adopting its current model after Hang saw an opportunity to help law firms handle mass arbitration. Firms accustomed to class actions could struggle with the work required to manage large numbers of individual claimants, he said. “It’s just really inefficient for them to try to build workflows around 10,000 claimants or 100,000 claimants,” Hang said. Chariot handles parts of that administrative work, while its partner firms handle the legal claims. The startup charges the firms flat service fees, and they work on a contingency basis. Hang emphasizes that since it’s not a law firm, Chariot itself doesn’t file claims. It helps consumers pursue a variety of claims. Those claims include allegations that websites or apps tracked their information without consent, that companies added fees during checkout, or that businesses made subscriptions easy to start but difficult to cancel, for example. Finding evidence and drawing objections Chariot starts by looking for potential cases involving privacy violations, hidden fees and other consumer complaints. Its software scans public records, including federal court filings, and uses AI to analyze the allegations and prepare research for its partner law firms. That research includes legal memos based on publicly filed complaints. Chariot is also developing tools to track changes in laws and court decisions that could affect whether a case can proceed. The work remains in the early stages, with the goal of automating more of the research that associates and paralegals would otherwise do, according to Hang. Chariot reviews a few hundred potential cases each month, he said. It tests ads for about 30 potential cases to gauge whether it can find consumers who may have a claim, then selects roughly 10 to pursue more extensively with its partner law firms. Each case can involve many individual consumers, whom Chariot reaches through advertising and partnerships with consumer financial technology companies. To determine whether they have a claim, consumers must provide information to help assess it. For example, in the case of a data breach, that could be a notice from the company saying their information was exposed. For a hidden-fee complaint, it could include what they purchased, when they bought it, and how much they paid. Chariot is building AI tools to help review that supporting information and determine whether a consumer has a claim, according to Hang. The required evidence, and the difficulty of verifying it, varies by the type of alleged violation. The startup plans to make that step easier by allowing users to connect their email accounts so its software can look for relevant documents, rather than asking consumers to fill out forms.  Hang estimates that such improvements could help the company handle 10x to 100x its current claim volume. Companies push back Not everyone welcomes Chariot’s approach. Advertising for potential claimants has brought strong objections from some of the companies involved. In fact, Chariot has received cease-and-desist letters challenging, among other things, its use of company names and trademarks in ads, noted Hang. But he asserts that identifying those businesses is necessary to reach people who used their products or services. “As a part of our business, we need to mention the name of the company that has this alleged violation,” he said. Chariot reviews the letters with legal counsel and complies with demands it considers valid, Hang said. He declined to name specific companies for this article. His broader goal is to make alleged consumer abuses more costly for businesses. If more affected customers pursue compensation, he reasons, companies will have a stronger financial incentive to change those practices. “We want to make unethical unprofitable,” he said. Mike Dodd , general partner at Silverton, told Crunchbase News via email that his firm was attracted to Chariot’s vertical AI approach to working with law firms, which he called “exciting and defensible.” “It’s a greenfield market with space to expand horizontally and eventually into a generalized consumer legal AI solution,” he wrote. The firm was also drawn to what Dodd described as “a business model that aligns capitalistic incentives with access to justice.” “When a company breaks the law and breaks what it promises to its consumers, the consumer rarely seeks justice,” he added. “Chariot has built the technology to make individual consumer claims work at scale, and the team to operate it in a category where execution is genuinely hard.” Related Crunchbase query: Global Legal And Legal Tech Startup Funding In 2026 Global Venture Funding To AI Startups In 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman

Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks. While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away , Clare V. , Monica + Andy , Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers . The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support. Planning campaigns To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems. Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive , Meta and Google , then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign. Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run. From there, teams can use the software to plan campaigns, draft marketing materials and assign work, with suggested campaigns and reports also delivered through Slack or email. Herrin said the lack of broader-picture context with other AI tools frustrated her. For example, a tool might identify a Fourth of July sale as a successful promotion and suggest repeating it. “Hey, no, I can’t. It’s not Fourth of July. We don’t have the inventory anymore,” she recalled thinking. In one case, Herrin described how Marklo identified a color trending on social media and a matching handbag a retailer had in stock but hadn’t promoted recently. It offered to plan a post based on one that had performed well before. Latico Leathers offers another example of how a brand uses Marklo. The company used the software to plan a month’s worth of marketing in one day, a process that had previously taken most of a week across meetings, spreadsheets and five tools, according to Herrin. In the end, humans review and approve Marklo’s proposed work. The company says it does not use customer data to train AI models. As for its revenue model, Marklo plans to charge a monthly subscription fee, with additional charges based on usage. For now, brands can install and try it for free. “I’m very passionate about small and medium businesses, and I want to make it accessible to every single brand that runs on Shopify,” Herrin told Crunchbase News in an interview, “so that they can operate like a big brand.” A change of direction The decision to build Marklo followed a change in how Herrin thought about Stella & Dot’s future. That company began as a way for women to earn money on their own schedules by hosting trunk shows in their own homes. It expanded into apparel and skincare and paid out more than $500 million to its sellers, Herrin said. “For me, it was never about the jewelry,” she told Crunchbase News. When COVID-19 put a stop to in-home gatherings, business dropped 80% almost overnight. Herrin also realized that women who might once have signed up to sell Stella & Dot products suddenly had other options. They could promote multiple brands as influencers or open their own Shopify stores. She described Stella & Dot as “the COVID victim that had pre-existing conditions.” Rather than rebuild the old model, Herrin sold the businesses and brands separately. Later, she bought back the Stella & Dot brand to sell through a different channel and test Marklo. She was also reconsidering what she wanted to do next. As she approached her 50th birthday, Herrin questioned whether she would choose to start the same business again. “As an entrepreneur, you don’t just start a business; you start a life,” she said. She still wanted to help people build businesses. What had changed was the problem she wanted to solve: Opening an online store had become easier, but managing its marketing still meant gathering information from several systems and coordinating the next campaign. “The mission was the same, but the solution needed to evolve,” Herrin said. A return to venture capital For Marklo, Herrin also returned to venture funding after relying more on profits to grow Stella & Dot. She had raised venture capital for her first company, which became WeddingChannel.com , but came away feeling that it had raised too much money. She took a different approach with Stella & Dot, building it with about $2 million in capital and a focus on profitability. “Here’s a new growth strategy,” Herrin recalled thinking. “How about profits?” With Marklo, she wanted to hire engineers and develop the software faster. Its 11-person team includes engineers who previously worked at Shopify and Google. She also sought investors with commerce experience. “Raising capital isn’t just about having money for expenses,” Herrin said. “It’s about bringing a brain trust together.” Experience as ‘the customer she’s building for’ Kirsten Green , founder and managing partner of Forerunner Ventures, said Herrin’s experience building Stella & Dot was a central reason for backing Marklo. “Jessica uniquely has been the customer that she’s building for right now at every stage, from starting a brand to having a brand at scale,” Green told Crunchbase News in an interview. That experience gives Herrin firsthand knowledge of where teams lose time, which decisions affect profitability and what brands need before trusting new technology, she added. While AI in general makes it easier to produce marketing content, Green sees the greater opportunity in helping brands decide on what exactly to promote, as well as in understanding the impact on margins and how to grow in ways consistent with their identity. Marklo, she said, incorporates the judgment needed to turn business data into useful recommendations. The opportunity comes as AI is taking a larger share of investment in the broader sales and marketing sector . Startups in sales, marketing and customer relationship management raised $7.5 billion across 830 rounds globally this year through mid-September, with most of that investment going to companies in Crunchbase’s AI-related categories. Funding is on pace to finish below 2025’s $11.1 billion, while deal volume could fall for a fourth straight year — a sign that investors are concentrating their bets in fewer companies. “It’s one thing to collect the information; it’s another thing to understand how to present it and how to recommend an action against it,” Green added. The investor also pointed to Marklo’s ability to serve businesses at different stages, noting that coordination becomes more complex and information harder to share as brands grow. As such, the prospect of software that can grow alongside its customers was another draw. Green said she also valued Herrin’s decision to develop Marklo alongside brands already using it, giving the company customer feedback before its broader launch. “I like the fact that she built this product while it was being used,” she said. payload.text: By Daniel Kjellén A first venture usually follows a well-worn playbook: a gap in the market, obsessive refinement of concept and pitch, eventual conviction that the solution is as bulletproof as it is revolutionary. Then, the dreaded phase of product-market fit. Instead of building the future of an entire industry, you find yourself forced to focus on a narrow use case and spend the first invaluable years proving that your idea can make money and scale. The grand vision gets put on pause. For most founders, this journey is the only one available. After all, investors are betting on someone who has never built a company before, so a small check and a narrow product limit what everyone stands to lose. But some ambitions need total commitment from the start, and having built a company before helps when taking them on. Lessons from the front line Daniel Kjellén, CEO and co-founder of Freda. After selling my first venture, Tink , to Visa for €1.8 billion (about $1.9 billion USD) in 2022, I found myself in a new position — and it wasn’t horizontal on a sun lounger. My co-founder Fredrik Hedberg and I had a real war chest of our own, and a brand-new entrepreneurial bug. For the first time in our lives, we had the experience and the resources to undertake something truly world-changing. Compliance is a gauntlet that any founder will be painfully familiar with. Scaling Tink across Europe, to 700 people operating under a host of regulators, my team and I got used to tearing our hair out over small wording tweaks, reviews that dragged on for months, and perpetual uncertainty that stopped us from iterating fast and boldly. Products were often delayed by months, a slip that meant the world in an industry moving as fast as ours. A problem with too many heads Compliance was a problem that could never be solved piecemeal. Every company’s obligations depend on a million different factors, each of which sits in a different part of the business that rarely talks to one another. Legal tracks regulations; another department oversees how they are implemented. Product teams make their own calls on features, and yet another team opens a case to check whether it was compliant. Policies, standards and regulations belong to other departments entirely, and those are usually the part of a silo a compliance startup builds for — a clear buyer and a budget. “Solving compliance” was a mission akin to fighting the Hydra: cut off one head and two more grow back. There is no minimum viable product here. Fixing one head changes nothing. What it takes is a maximum viable product from day one. Why the second time is different In recent years, we’ve seen a series of inspiring examples of successful founders coming back to take on new problems. Stockholm knows this well: alumni of Spotify and Klarna have gone on to found and back a long list of new companies, using the credibility from their first successes to try something harder. The second time around, capital and access both come easier. A successful first exit opens doors to talent, partners and investors that we simply didn’t have with Tink. It is a fantastic opportunity, and one I’m grateful for. You get to bring every lesson from what went well and what went badly, and you start with a real tailwind when people want to work with you and back you. Money also means you can fund the full build yourself, so no investor asks you to shrink the idea before you’ve tested it. Maximum viable product Experience and capital used to get you only so far. Ten years ago, building something this broad would still have needed hundreds of people of various backgrounds, and many years. Language models have changed that. Our team today is 22 strong and growing, and ships at a pace I could only have dreamed of when we first built Tink. We also feel we’ve grown thicker skin from the bruises of our first 15 years as entrepreneurs. You know the setbacks are coming, and you know that a venture is never a one-man sprint but a team marathon. None of that guarantees success. But it’s a good place to start if you want to stand your ground and build your biggest vision yet. Daniel Kjellén is the CEO and co-founder of Freda , the Stockholm-based AI-native compliance company that came out of stealth in September 2026. He previously co-founded the open banking platform Tink in 2012 and led it as CEO through its growth to a multimarket operation with around 700 employees before its €1.8 billion acquisition by Visa in 2022. payload.text: A total of 38 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in September, adding $71 billion in value to the board. Semiconductors, financial services and space technology led for new counts with the remainder hailing from a broad swath of industries including biotech, AI infrastructure, AI training, security and frontier labs. Twenty-one of last month’s new unicorns are U.S. headquartered. Six new unicorns joined the board from China and three from the U.K., while Canada, Saudi Arabia, Japan, Israel, Italy, Finland, Germany and Bulgaria each added one new unicorn. Through September, 311 companies have joined the board so far this year, putting 2026 on track to be the second-highest year for new unicorn creation, following only the venture peak year of 2021, when counts topped 600. Several companies already on the board stand out for significant valuation increases via new raises last month. They include San Francisco-based Cognition , developer of AI for software engineering, which saw its value climb to $48 billion, up from $26 billion only four months earlier. Data center provider Crusoe was valued at $31 billion last month, up from $10 billion a year ago. And Paris-based frontier lab Mistral was valued at $24.4 billion in its more recent funding, up from $13.7 billion a year ago. New unicorns in September Here are September’s 38 new unicorn companies: Semiconductors Fab2 , an Austin-based semiconductor manufacturing startup, closed a $500 million Series A at a $3.7 billion valuation, led by Fundomo . The 3-year-old company builds compact chip factories and develops their manufacturing equipment internally, aiming to make semiconductor production more accessible. Celero Communications , an Irvine, California-based semiconductor company, raised a $275 million Series C, valuing it above $3 billion and bringing total funding to $415 million. Atreides Management , Valor Equity Partners and CapitalG led the round. The 2-year-old company develops digital signal processing chips for high-speed optical connectivity in AI infrastructure. Micronano Core , a Hangzhou-based AI chip developer, announced a $149 million Series C. Its IoT inference chips combine memory and computing to reduce power consumption and data movement. The 5-year-old company was valued at $1 billion. Evas Intelligence , a Beijing-based AI chip company, raised $298 million at a valuation of $2.2 billion. The 4-year-old company develops AI computing chips using the open RISC-V architecture. SiMa.ai , a San Jose, California-based developer of specialized AI chips and software, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation, co-led by Fidelity and Amplify Partners , bringing total funding to $500 million. The proceeds for the 8-year-old company will support its software platform and next-generation hardware for robots, vehicles and drones. Financial services OG , a Texas-based prediction-market platform, announced a strategic partnership with Robinhood , which will take an equity stake following OG’s separation from Crypto.com . The less than 1-year-old company was valued at $5 billion. The investment amount was not disclosed; the partnership will route Robinhood event-contract trading through OG’s regulated exchange and clearing infrastructure. Saudi Arabia-based Barq , a digital payments company, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion valuation. Investors included Noon Investments , Sohar International and M20 Capital . The 3-year-old company has processed more than $117 billion in 2 years. Ridgeline , a Nevada-based financial software company, raised a $250 million Series E at a $1.43 billion valuation led by founder and chairman Dave Duffield . The 8-year-old company provides an AI-based investment management platform for asset and wealth managers. Félix , a Miami-based remittance platform for Latino immigrants operating through WhatsApp , secured $200 million in financing: an $87 million Series C equity round led by Andreessen Horowitz valued at $1.4 billion and $113 million in debt from General Catalyst ’s Customer Value Fund. The 5-year-old company plans to expand to lending and add to its Latin American reach . Space technology Munich-based space company The Exploration Co. raised a $450 million Series C, co-led by Bessemer Venture Partners , Atomico and EQT at a valuation of $2 billion. The financing for the 5-year-old company will advance its reusable Nyx spacecraft for an International Space Station mission and support development of its Storm rocket engine. Hubble Network , a Seattle-based satellite connectivity company, raised a $200 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Smith Point Capital , bringing total funding to approximately $300 million. The 5-year-old company enables standard Bluetooth devices to connect directly to satellites for tracking and sensor-data applications. Oxfordshire, U.K-based Open Cosmos , a satellite company, secured $346 million, co-led by ETF Partners and Lightrock , valued at $1 billion. The 11-year-old company manufactures satellites and provides infrastructure, connectivity, Earth observation and intelligence services. Bulgaria-based EnduroSat , a satellite company, raised $205 million in a round co-led by Riot Ventures and Atreides Management , reaching a $1 billion valuation. The 11-year-old company has raised financing that will expand standardized spacecraft production, including new manufacturing capacity in the U.S. and Europe. Biotechnology and medical devices Alzheon , a Framingham, Massachusetts-based developer of treatments for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders, raised around $79 million. The   13-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. Investors were not disclosed. Shanghai-based Anew Labs , an AI drug discovery company, raised $290 million at a $1.5 billion valuation following its spinoff from ByteDance . HSG , IDG Capital , Hillhouse Capital and 5Y Capital co-led the round. Anew develops tools for biomolecular prediction and drug discovery; ByteDance retained a 56% stake. Precision Neuroscience , a New York-based brain-computer interface developer, closed a $250 million Series D, bringing total funding to $430 million and reaching a valuation of approximately $1 billion. Pershing Square and Ackman Oxman Institute led the round. The 5-year-old company is building a brain–computer interface that is minimally invasive and removable. Toronto-based Biossil , a biotechnology company, raised $153 million at a $1 billion valuation led by the OpenAI Startup Fund , with participation from Founders Fund and other investors. The 3-year-old company uses AI to identify abandoned drug candidates that could succeed under different treatment approaches. The financing will expand clinical development and support additional drug acquisitions. AI and internet infrastructure Gimlet Labs , a San Francisco-based AI cloud infrastructure company, raised a $300 million Series B at a $3 billion valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz . The 3-year-old company distributes AI inference workloads across different types of chips to improve performance and efficiency. It announced in March that its customers include one of the leading frontier labs. Helsinki-based Verda , an AI cloud company, raised a $189 million Series B led by Emergence Capital . The financing valued the 6-year-old company above $1 billion with total funding over $450 million. The company manages physical data centers along with its cloud platform. London-based CDN77 , an internet infrastructure company supporting content delivery for large streaming, gaming and software companies, raised $570 million in its first external financing led by CVC Capital Partners . The 15-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. AI training Micro1 , a San Francisco-based AI training-data company, raised more than $100 million led by Dream Ventures at a $4 billion valuation, an eightfold increase from its valuation in September 2025. The 4-year-old company recruits and vets specialists who create training and evaluation data for AI developers. Forbes reported that participants included two frontier AI laboratories and two x.AI co-founders. AfterQuery , a San Francisco-based provider of expert-created AI training data, reached a $3.2 billion valuation in September, more than 10x its valuation five months earlier, according to Forbes . The funding amount and lead investor were not publicly disclosed. The 1-year-old company’s datasets capture professional reasoning in fields such as software engineering, law and finance. AfterQuery was part of the Winter 2025 Y Combinator batch. Robotics and autonomous driving Shanghai Zaofu Intelligent Technology , the Shanghai-based operator of Hello’s robotaxi business, raised about $100 million at a valuation close to $3 billion. Shanghai State-owned Capital Investment fund led the round. The financing to the 1-year-old company will support a 10,000-GPU computing cluster, AI model development and commercialization of Level 4 autonomous driving. Lyte AI , a Sunnyvale, California-based robotics perception company, raised a $165 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Maverick Silicon . Founded by former Apple and PrimeSense engineers, the 5-year-old company combines custom chips, sensors and spatial software to help robots perceive their surroundings. The financing will accelerate deployments across logistics, manufacturing and inspection applications. Health insurance Angle Health , a San Francisco-based health benefits company, announced a $200 million Series C at a $2.7 billion valuation. Vitruvian Partners led the financing. It also includes $400 million in secondary financing for existing investors. The 7-year-old company provides a benefits platform using AI to make healthcare more affordable for small and midsize employers. The company services 5,000 businesses. Thatch , a San Francisco-based health benefits platform, raised a $108 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation. Investors included The General Partnership , Index Ventures , General Catalyst and Andreessen Horowitz . The 5-year-old company helps employers provide individualized health budgets for employees to select their own medical plans. It has 5,000 employers utilizing its service. Energy and EV infrastructure China-based NIO Power , a battery-swapping and charging company, agreed to a strategic transaction that gives Geely Auto a 30% stake. Geely will contribute its Yiyi battery-swapping operation and a $95 million investment. The 9-year-old company was valued around $2.4 billion. TAR , an Austin-based developer of off-grid power systems for AI data centers, raised a $120 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation, led by Spark Capital . The less than 1-year-old company builds modular systems for renewable energy and battery systems as data-center operators seek access to electricity. AI applications Brahma AI raised $150 million led by Multiples , at a valuation just over $2 billion. The 3-year-old company, headquartered in London with offices in Los Angeles and Mumbai, built an enterprise audiovisual content platform for media, advertising, sports and healthcare customers. The financing will support research, commercial expansion and a larger Silicon Valley presence. Sequen , a New York-based AI ranking and personalization company, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.44 billion valuation, led by Prysm Capital . The 2-year-old company’s software helps enterprises respond to customer behavior in real time, improving the relevance of recommendations. Cybersecurity Rome-based Exein , a cybersecurity company protecting connected devices and autonomous machines, raised $270 million at a $1.7 billion valuation, led by Headline . The financing to the 8-year-old company will support U.S. and Asia-Pacific expansion and development of AI security models. Tel Aviv-based Guardio , a consumer cybersecurity company, raised $40 million at a $1.1 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $167 million. Wiz co-founder Assaf Rappaport joined existing investors including Ion Crossover Partners and Union Tech Ventures , among others. The 8-year-old company protects consumers against phishing, scams, malicious websites and AI-generated fraud. AI models Beijing-based Naive AI , a language-model startup, raised $120 million reaching a valuation of $1.4 billion. Investors include Tencent , IDG Capital , Matrix Partners China and HSG . The less than 1-year-old company raised $400 million across three rounds so far this year, before releasing its first public model. Arcee AI , a San Francisco-based developer of open-weight foundation models, announced a $150 million Series B led by Vista Equity Partners , Cambium Capital Partners and Emergence Capital , valuing the company above $1 billion. The financing will support the 3-year-old company’s Trinity models and products for customizing and operating them. Manufacturing and construction software CADDi , an AI company for manufacturing with dual headquarters in Tokyo and Chicago, raised a $114 million Series D at a $1.2 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $234 million. Investors included Moore Strategic Ventures and Coreline Ventures . The 9-year-old company’s platform organizes design and procurement and production; the financing will deepen its technology and accelerate North American expansion. Kahua , a Georgia-based construction software company, secured a growth investment of $250 million led by Bain Capital Tech Opportunities , valuing it above $1 billion. The 17-year-old company manages construction projects, with the investment supporting its AI capability build out and commercial growth. Defense technology Covenant , a Washington, D.C.-based defense company, emerged from stealth with $250 million raised across three rounds at a valuation above $1 billion. The 2-year-old company develops long-range cruise missiles with manufacturing in Texas, Germany and Israel. Backers who have led across three rounds include Andreessen Horowitz , Founders Fund , Lux Capital , 8VC 1 , Lightspeed Venture Partners and Aleph . Food Medici Brands , the New York-based parent of consumer food brands David Protein and HallPass, raised a $250 million Series B at a $2.25 billion valuation. Greenoaks and Valor Equity Partners co-led the round. The financing to the 2-year-old company will expand retail distribution, develop new products and support additional brands. New companies are added to the Unicorn Board as they reach the $1 billion valuation mark as part of a funding round. The unicorn board does not reflect internal company valuations — such as those set via a 409a process for employee stock options — as these differ from, and are more likely to be lower than, a priced funding round. payload.text: By Nnamdi Okike You have likely never heard of Tosin Eniolorunda . You should have. Over the past decade, Tosin and his team built Moniepoint into the operating system for more than 6 million Nigerian businesses, processing over $300 billion a year , or 39% of Nigeria’s digital payments volume and 8 out of every 10 in-person payments . As a Nigerian American, I’ve witnessed my father make trips to Western Union to send money back home for decades, and I experienced Nigeria’s fee-laden payment system when visiting the country. Moniepoint is transforming that system. Nnamdi Okike, co-founder and managing partner of 645 Ventures. Moniepoint is not alone. Sea Limited , Grab , Kaspi , Yassir , Nubank 1 — these are companies most Americans have never heard of, despite them being worth several tens or hundreds of billions, following the trail blazed by Tencent , Alibaba and MercadoLibre . These are super apps that bundle banking, commerce, ride-hailing and bill pay into one trusted application. The idea never took hold in the U.S. for one reason: trust is cheap here. With 96% of households already banked , a specialist app inherits the credibility of the financial system. Where trust is cheap, there is no need for a super app. Build trust first In emerging markets, trust is the whole problem. Four conditions tend to precede a super app: High mobile penetration, which makes distribution cheap; weak incumbent competition; poor existing financial services; and the condition most investors screen past, a financial crisis severe enough to strip incumbents of legitimacy. These populations are not merely underbanked. They were harmed, and the institutions that harmed them still hold the market. Brazil froze roughly 80% of bank deposits and financial investments for 18 months in 1990 in an effort to break hyperinflation. The banking consolidation that followed left five banks holding about 80% of banking assets and charging card rates north of 300% . That was the void Nubank was born into. Kazakhstan went through it twice: savings erased by inflation in the thousands of percent when the ruble zone collapsed in 1993, then a 2007–09 banking crisis in which the country’s largest bank, BTA, holding roughly a quarter of the system’s assets, was nationalized and defaulted amid allegations of multibillion-dollar fraud. Kaspi grew into that void. Southeast Asia’s 1997 crisis was harsher still. Indonesia closed 16 banks in a single announcement, the rupiah lost about 85% of its value, and output fell 13 %. Two decades later roughly half of Indonesian adults still had no bank account, which enabled Sea to build Shopee and SeaMoney into that gap. Kaspi also answers the objection I hear most from American investors, which is that these markets are too small to produce large exits. Kazakhstan has only 20 million people, and according to company filings , around 14 million — nearly 70% of its population — use Kaspi. The average user transacts roughly 77 times a month . It earns $9 billion of revenue at 56% EBITDA margins, and its enterprise value is over $17 billion . Depth of spend, not population, sets the ceiling. Compare Nubank to Chime . Nubank has 14x the customers, 127 million to Chime’s 9.5 million , about 7x the revenue and a market capitalization more than 6x larger. Nubank has brought over 31 million previously unbanked Brazilians into the financial system . A technology applied in an overlooked market with a large unaddressed pain point can build a bigger and more defensible company than the same technology applied in a rich one. Screen for the four conditions and a few markets stand out as places where the next super app could emerge: Bangladesh: Five banks looted from the inside for years before the 2024 change in government exposed them , with the government now promising to pay 7.5 million savers whose money is gone. Egypt: Repeated devaluations of the pound between 2016 and 2024, shrinking savings held at banks the state itself owns. Vietnam: Savers pulled 80% of deposits out of one major bank in 2022 after its owner was arrested in a $24 billion fraud. Pakistan: A near-default and 38% inflation in 2023 , then government-built rails and a national ID that makes onboarding nearly costless. One boundary condition: The crisis must be severe enough to delegitimize incumbents but contained enough that the currency and payment rails still work. The first generation of super apps created enormous value for the investors who backed them early. In 2001, the South African media company Naspers paid roughly $34 million for a 46.5% stake in Tencent, a stake later worth more than $100 billion and one of the best tech investments ever made . Sequoia Capital ’s investment in Nubank’s $2 million seed round, combined with its lead Series A investment, was worth $7 billion at the company’s IPO . The second generation is scaling now. The third will be built on stablecoins and AI technologies, in Abidjan, Buenos Aires, Karachi and Lagos, by founders like Tosin Eniolorunda who will play an increasingly important role in the growth of emerging market economies. Nnamdi Okike is co-founder and managing partner of 645 Ventures , where he oversees the firm’s investing strategy, governance and compliance, with a focus on fintech and enterprise technology. Since co-founding 645 Ventures in 2014, he has invested in and partnered with companies including RentSpree , Setpoint , Sequence , Solidus Labs , Order and Uptiq . Previously, he was an investor at Insight Partners , where he invested in 19 companies and had nine exits representing more than $9 billion in exit value. title: whatsapp-mcp
summary: WhatsApp MCP running free on Cloudflare

extra.author: zoozla
extra.original_title: Show HN: WhatsApp MCP running free on Cloudflare

story_text.value:
I wanted my humble Claude on mobile to access my WhatsApp messages but the only options I could find either required WhatsApp Business or an actual server to run Baileys on.

I wanted to run it for free on ClaudeFlare and with my personal WhatsApp account, so I built this.

Important feature - it connects to your Google account as well as WhatsApp to grab the names of all your WhatsApp contacts, otherwise you get only phone numbers for many of them and search doesn't work properly.

This is a single user install because it's both gray area and very private - so point your agent at the repo and let it set things up.

title: Bullet Script (bs)
summary: a Lisp(y) VM for shmup bullet patterns

extra.author: ellg
extra.original_title: Show HN: Bullet Script (bs) – a Lisp(y) VM for shmup bullet patterns

story_text.value:
I'm a huge fan of an old project called BulletML which was a way of describing shmup (typically bullet hell) patterns in a kinda weird and clunky XML format.

I, however, think sexprs + a little lisp magic can make this idea a lot more fun so I made bullet-script.

You can check out a live repl (ctrl+enter submits the buffer) + demo on the linked site in this submission and you can also check out a language guide here: https://bs.ell.dev/guide/

I'd love to see what you folks can make! If you made a cool pattern please link and share it here!

title: legendofhyrule
summary: The Zelda timeline to catch up before the Ocarina of Time remake

extra.author: jsomau
extra.original_title: Show HN: The Zelda timeline to catch up before the Ocarina of Time remake

story_text.value:
I made this ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake which comes out in 17 days. I remember the feeling of playing it as a kid but I hadn’t kept up with the story so I built a timeline to catch up before the Door of Time reopens.

Nintendo’s own timeline is the authority here (Hyrule Historia and their chronicle page). The fun part was rethinking how to visualize it. It branches at the end of Ocarina into three eras depending on whether Link wins or loses, so each era is its own thread on the cloth. The threads meet again much later with Breath of the Wild.

I had a lot of help from Claude. I’d often thought about building things like this but never found the time between the day job and the rest of life.

title: CallSitter
summary: bot that answers my calls and wastes scammers' time

extra.author: szert
extra.original_title: Show HN: CallSitter – bot that answers my calls and wastes scammers' time

story_text.value:
Anyone else get a lot of dumb scam calls?

These days I mostly get them on my mobile. I used to just ignore them, but then I got fed up and built a bot that answers my calls and wastes their time.

It runs on OpenAI Live 1. Jev classifies each call as spam, scam or genuine and steers the bot accordingly.

title: Esp32sim
summary: Run ESP32 firmware in the browser

extra.author: joakimeriksson
extra.original_title: Show HN: Esp32sim – Run ESP32 firmware in the browser

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I’ve been working on esp32sim, an open-source ESP32 emulator that runs in the browser.

The fun part of the demo is that there is no ESP32 involved — the firmware is executing in the emulator.

The goal is to make ESP32 software easier to experiment with, test and simulate without always needing physical hardware connected.

Source: https://github.com/mikroverk/esp32sim

I made a short video showing it in action: https://youtu.be/waoWFilTWEc

I’m particularly interested in feedback from embedded developers: what would an emulator like this need to support before you’d actually use it for development, testing or CI?

title.value: Show HN: Esp32sim – Run ESP32 firmware in the browser

payload.author: joakimeriksson
payload.story_text:
Hi HN,

I’ve been working on esp32sim, an open-source ESP32 emulator that runs in the browser.

The fun part of the demo is that there is no ESP32 involved — the firmware is executing in the emulator.

The goal is to make ESP32 software easier to experiment with, test and simulate without always needing physical hardware connected.

Source: https://github.com/mikroverk/esp32sim

I made a short video showing it in action: https://youtu.be/waoWFilTWEc

I’m particularly interested in feedback from embedded developers: what would an emulator like this need to support before you’d actually use it for development, testing or CI?

Building trust in AI agents: A production-ready evaluation framework with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: The North Star Every organization racing to deploy AI agents faces the same reckoning: an agent that demos beautifully can quietly degrade in production, and by the time a human notices, the trust is already broken. Where traditional software fails loudly, agents fail softly. They return an answer that looks confident, reads fluently, and is wrong. When that answer drives a real business decision, the cost is not a broken feature. It’s a broken relationship with the user. That’s the quality problem at its core. The challenge is therefore not building agents that work once, but proving they keep working, at scale, across every sub-agent, every workflow, and every release. The teams that win the agent era will be the ones who treat quality not as a final QA step but as the operating system of the agent itself: continuously measured, automatically defended, and improved with every interaction. In this post, we show how we built a continuous quality loop for production-ready agentic solutions at scale using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Business problem The solution uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and other AWS services for internal use, so sellers and sales leaders can ask business questions in plain English from Amazon Quick.

title: Introducing Reflection Beam: an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS
summary: Reflection AI introduced Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks such as maintaining code, using tools, interpreting results, and completing multi-step workflows. The open-weight release gives developers and researchers control over the runtime, deployment environment, and customization process. In this post, we explain Reflection’s vision and show how you can deploy Beam on AWS. Start with an Amazon SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint for a fully managed path. When you need Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure, use Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM. We also explain how Beam’s 501 billion total parameters shape checkpoint storage, weight memory, sharding, and parallelism, while its 23 billion active parameters influence per-token compute. At launch, Beam is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). Reflection’s vision for open intelligence Reflection’s mission is to make intelligence open and accessible to all through open model weights, published research, and open source software. Its full AI stack spans models, core software, production infrastructure, and applications. Beam brings this approach to developers building software engineering and agentic systems. summary: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 新版本上线：许愿式编程一键成真 10 月 17 日，DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 更新至 V4.1-Flash-1017 版本，官方网页端、APP 与 API 模型已同步变更为新模型。相比上一版本的 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash，新模型在各方面的基准测试中取得了长足的提升。 在提升性能的同时，模型的任务运行时间与输出长度还缩短了，让用户能够以更低成本、更快速度完成任务，在多个 Harness 下达到了新的性能-费用帕累托最优。 特别地，此次优化着重针对 DeepSeek Harness、腾讯 CodeBuddy、WorkBuddy 等平台框架进行了优化。（消息来源：DeepSeek） 马斯克盯上了砍价生意 号称一年为全球省下 6 万亿美元 10 月 17 日消息，特斯拉创始人马斯克在社交平台 X 发文称，团队正投入大量资源，开发面向商业场景的专用议价机器人（Hagglebot）。 Hagglebot 是依托 Grok 打造的软件 AI Bot，主打企业议价场景，和普通对话 AI 定位完全不同。目前马斯克没有放出太多细节，这套 AI 具体怎么议价、支持哪些交易场景、何时上线、怎么收费，都还没有官宣。 马斯克表示，「我们认为该产品能够将企业成本效率提升 5% 乃至更高。如果放到全球 GDP 的维度测算，每年可节省的成本规模最高可达 6 万亿美元。」 他还进一步指出，凡是使用 Grok 的企业，都能获得立即可量化的竞争优势。（消息来源：快科技） 要么不用工具，要么交出内容？Meta 新条款引争议 Gizmodo 报道，社交巨头 Meta 更新 Meta Business Suite 商业账号服务条款，新规将于 10 月 30 日正式落地。 按照新协议，企业开通 Facebook、Instagram 商业账号，就自动授予 Meta 抓取自家网站公开内容的权利，且没有设置独立关闭退出通道。即便企业网站通过 robots.txt 规则屏蔽网络爬虫，也无法阻止本次基于商业账号协议授权下的内容采集。 过去 Meta 若要使用出版商、企业网页素材训练 AI，需要单独签署版权授权协议。而本次条款改动，把内容授权绑定商业工具使用资格。不少法律从业者表示，大量中小企业在开通商业推广账号时，并不会仔细阅读冗长的服务协议，在不知情的状态下完成内容授权。 Meta 解释，抓取网页内容旨在提升 Meta AI 的回答准确度，企业既然使用平台商业服务，就应当开放网页内容使用权。但出版商与中小企业行业协会对此提出批评，认为新规等于逼迫企业二选一：要么放弃 Meta 商业营销工具，要么交出网站内容用于 AI 训练，绕过正常版权协商流程，损害内容方权益。（消息来源：环球科技） 英伟达黄仁勋称 AI 现在不是泡沫，安全不应成为减速理由 10 月 17 日消息，英国当地时间 10 月 14 日在伦敦接受彭博记者 Emily Chang 采访时，英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋表示当前 AI 需求远大于供给， 不认为现阶段处于「AI 泡沫」阶段，不过他也承认未来供给可能超过需求。 在采访中，黄仁勋表示：「泡沫发生在供给超过需求的时候。最终供需会趋于平衡，而且在某个时候，供给可能会超过需求，但不是今天。今天，需求远远大于供给。」 面对 AI 云服务商 CoreWeave 引发的市场担忧，黄仁勋表示没有必要救助该公司，其财务状况会没问题。（消息来源：IT 之家） 华为全新子品牌「星芒」手机将主攻线上：性价比定位！ 10 月 17 日消息，近期多方传闻都提到，华为全新子品牌「星芒」手机即将登场。「星芒」手机将主攻线上，定位相对有性价比，目前已经规划了好几款新机，其中还有搭载主动散热风扇的版本。 品牌定位上，星芒被视作对标早年独立出去的荣耀，补齐华为长期空缺的线上中端区间，传闻产品搭载麒麟 8 系或 9 系自研芯片。 商标记录显示，华为早在 2023 年就已申请"星芒"相关商标，2026 年 7 月又提交新的申请，不过华为对外回应均为"请以官方信息为准"，品牌归属与方案目前仍属未经官方确认的传闻。（消息来源：快科技） iPhone 18 Pro Max 国内单周激活量近 90 万：全系销量超 400 万 10 月 17 日消息，iPhone 18 Pro Max 再度刷新纪录，在 2026 年第 41 周（10 月 5 日至 10 月 11 日）单周单品国内激活接近 90 万台。 此外，iPhone 18 Pro 系列双杯累计销量目前已经超过 400 万台。 从产品结构来看，大屏、大内存配置的 iPhone 18 Pro Max 占据绝对主力，出货量占比超过全系列总量的 50%，消费者选择顶配版本的意愿强于往年新品发布周期。 另外，近期发布的安卓旗舰机型因关键零部件成本上升普遍提价，万元价位段内安卓顶配与 iPhone Pro 系列的价格差距明显收窄，客观上强化了苹果高端机型的价值感知。 相当一部分原本倾向安卓顶配的用户转向新款 iPhone，叠加高端消费群体对价格变动敏感度较低，共同支撑了持续激活量。（消息来源：快科技） AI 小海卖惨骗姨姨妈妈：高价带货专坑老人同情心钱 近期短视频平台上，出现不少视频有类似的内容：一个叫小海的小伙子脸色憔悴，对着镜头说自己父亲生病欠了债，没办法才出来卖点货还债，一口一个姨姨妈妈叫得格外亲热。 更离谱的是，这并不是一个小海，网上一搜就会有几十个叫小海、小涛、小宇的账号，长得各不一样，故事却大同小异，全是清一色的卖惨带货。 据报道，这其实是批量复制的 AI 带货演员。 有账号运营者表示，这套小海的模式和话术是公开的，人人都能用，选对中老年赛道，一天赚两三千算是少的。 这个是一年前另一批广告的延续，当时，一批身着正装、言语温情的中年「AI 王建国」，被精准推送给缺乏陪伴的中老年女性。 而那是「AI 小海」只是「AI 王建国」身边的配角：「王建国的儿子小海」，曾向阿姨们倾诉自己因为没有妈妈而遭到校园霸凌，邀请阿姨们为父亲带来真正的幸福。 随着国家大力整治 AI 技术滥用乱象，各大短视频平台陆续关停部分「王建国」账号、清空相关视频。之后「王建国」的朋友、兄弟、领导，乃至女儿、儿子等配角，被运营者陆续推到台前，试图再造一个王建国式的流量入口。 其中儿子「小海」成了最火的一个，他接过父亲的剧本，也接过同一批姨姨妈妈，开始又一轮精心设计的收割。（消息来源：快科技） 上汽荣威家越 07

title: 1 分钟售罄、发货排到明年，iPhone Duo 卖爆背后的真相
summary: 人们已经很多年没见过，苹果的新品被这样抢了。 10 月 16 日晚 8 点，苹果首款折叠屏 iPhone Duo 开启预购。社交媒体上流传的说法是， 开售 1 分钟，全型号库存就空了，京东、天猫页面相继显示售罄 。 大约 40 分钟后， 苹果官网的预计送达时间已经跳到了 2027 年 1 月底 。 几个小时后，大洋彼岸的美国东部时间上午 8 点，同样的剧情再演一遍。分析师 Max Weinbach 在 X 上说，纽约及周边、康涅狄格州的门店大约 3 分钟就被抢光。半小时内，美国所有配置的交付日期都变成了 1 月 25 日。eBay 上，一台 2TB 版的预购机挂出了 5000 美元的成交价，比官方价格高出 1800 美元。 这不是中国市场独有的狂热，而是一场苹果新品全球同步的抢购。 iPhone Duo 卖爆的背后，真的是产品太牛，创新性十足，还是产能不足逼出的热卖？ 「秒罄」这两个字，其实藏着两个完全不同的故事。一个关于需求，一个关于产能。 太整齐的交付日期 先看一个容易被忽略的细节。 iPhone Duo 这次在美国、中国、英国、德国、日本、印度等约 70 个国家和地区同步开启预购 。开售之后，美国和英国最早的交付日期都是 1 月 25 日，国行显示的是 1 月底。 市场规模、消费习惯、竞争格局完全不同的几个国家，交付日期却几乎对齐。 这更像是苹果在全球范围内按配额统一分货的结果，而不是各地需求恰好一样旺。 换句话说，首批能放出来的货就那么多，分到每个市场的量都不大，哪里都是几分钟被抢完。 这一点从黄牛市场也能看出来。 国内顶配机型的加价被报到 7000 元以上，甚至有说法称破万 ；美国 1TB 和 2TB 两个版本的转售价都比官方价格高出约 1800 美元。以 2TB 版来算，美国的溢价幅度大约是五成多，和国内的情况相差无几。 两边的「热度」高度相似，恰恰说明真正决定热度上限的，是供给。 让人遗憾的产能 如果把时间拨回到一个多月前，iPhone Duo 的产能问题其实早有端倪。 日经亚洲 8 月底的报道称， 苹果当时每天只能生产「几百台」iPhone Duo ，远远低于一款常规 iPhone 新品的爬坡节奏。9 月中旬，界面新闻援引供应链消息称，富士康的组装良率只比 60% 高一点，要提升到成熟水平，可能还需要半年到一年。 问题的核心，在那枚特殊设计的铰链上。 供应链消息显示，iPhone Duo 的铰链由 100 多个零件组成，外盖还用到了 3D 打印工艺。原本的主力供应商安费诺产能没能达到苹果的预期，苹果随后加大了台湾新日兴的供货比例。屏幕这一侧也不轻松，三星显示的折叠 OLED 面板良率同样偏低，部分原因是苹果在最后阶段改了设计。 分析师 Jeff Pu 因此把 iPhone Duo 今年的出货预测从 700 万台下调到 600 万台。他给出的理由很直接，是铰链拖了后腿，而不是需求不足。 需要说明的是，60% 良率不等于卖出去的手机有四成是坏的，它意味着有相当比例的机器第一次组装没有通过苹果的品控，需要返工或报废，生产因此变得又慢又贵。 说白了，苹果选择了「宁可少卖，也不能卖坏」。对第一代折叠屏来说，这几乎是唯一正确的选择。 当然，这些消息大多来自匿名的供应链渠道，苹果并没有正式确认过。 想买的人，也是真的多 如果只是货少，iPhone Duo 的故事不会这么好看。 开售前，仅京东一个平台的预约人数就被报道突破 200 万，也有说法称超过 300 万。不管哪个数字更准确，都远远高于首批的货量。 更值得玩味的是价格。 iPhone Duo 国行 256GB 版起售价 15999 元，2TB 顶配是 26499 元；美版起售价 1999 美元，顶配 3199 美元，这是苹果历史上最贵的一部手机。 在一个连「贵」都不足以形容的价位上还能秒罄，抢的已经不只是一部折叠屏，而是苹果的品牌溢价。 还有一层原因是「等待」。 折叠屏这个品类已经卖了七年，三星、华为、荣耀、OPPO、vivo 轮番迭代，苹果却一直按兵不动。 这些年里，攒下了一大批「等苹果做了再说」的用户 。他们未必是折叠屏的忠实拥趸，但他们相信苹果会是那个把折叠屏「做对」的人。 资本市场显然也愿意相信这一点。Deepwater 的 Gene Munster 认为 iPhone Duo 首年出货可能接近 2000 万台，Bloomberg Intelligence 也表示销量将超过他们此前 1400 万台的预测。 不过 Counterpoint 和 TrendForce 给出的今年预测都在 500 万到 600 万台之间，几家机构的分歧之大，本身就说明了一件事。 苹果没有公布首批到底放出了多少货，所以「秒罄」能证明有人想买，却证明不了苹果能卖出多少台。 卖爆背后的不同故事 把中国和美国放在一起看，会发现同一场抢购背后，是两个完全不同的市场。 在美国，折叠屏是三星的地盘。三星自己的数据显示，Galaxy Z Fold 8 系列在美国的销量比上一代高出约 30%。对美国用户来说，iPhone Duo 更像是苹果给折叠屏这个品类「正名」，把一个小众品类推向大众。 在中国，故事要复杂得多。 国内折叠屏的主角是华为。Omdia 的数据显示，今年上半年全球书本式折叠屏市场，华为拿下了 57% 的份额。但整个中国折叠屏市场的日子并不好过，已经连续三个季度同比下滑，IDC 预计全年还会下降 26.7%，原因之一正是苹果折叠屏在中国的供货有限，很多人在观望。 这意味着，苹果在中国点燃的，是一个原本正在降温的品类。 更大的背景是，苹果在中国的整体表现其实比很多人想象中要好。今年三季度中国手机市场整体下滑 15.4%，苹果出货只下降了 4.3%，份额反而提升到 17.8%，仅次于华为的 21%。iPhone 18 Pro 系列首发三天，销量同比增长

title: iPhone Duo 一秒售罄，发货排到明年；马斯克：考虑自建电商平台；谷歌创始人：AI 正开始自己造自己
summary: 苹果官网 2026 年的 iPhone Duo 已售罄！发货日期排到明年 1 月 22 日 10 月 16 日，苹果首款折叠屏 iPhone Duo 于当晚 8 点开启线上预购，大量用户同时涌入苹果官网、Apple Store App 及天猫、京东等官方直营渠道，购买页面一度无法正常打开。开售一分钟左右，各大电商平台即显示该机型售罄。 目前官网仍可下单，预计发货时间排至 1 月 22 日，2026 年的备货已全部售罄。受折叠屏铰链、柔性内屏产能爬坡周期长于直板机型、首批备货有限叠加首发集中抢购影响，交期被拉长。后续随着产能释放，发货排期将逐步前移，已抢到 11 月、12 月批次的用户或提前半个月拿到新机。 该机型维修费用极高，非 AppleCare+用户更换内屏需 7998 元，外屏需 3198 元，电池维修费用达 1898 元，建议自用用户选购 AppleCare+。(来源：IT 之家） 马斯克回应 Grok Bot 被亚马逊封禁：不让 AI 智能体网购，就考虑自建电商平台 科技媒体 notateslaapp 10 月 15 日发布博文，报道称有用户反馈亚马逊阻止 Grok Bot 智能体在其平台下单之后，全球首富马斯克表示考虑打造一家与亚马逊竞争的公司。 该媒体指出特斯拉上月已将 Grok Bot 整合进车辆，用户可在通勤途中把下单任务交给 AI。用户无需亲自打开零售商网站，即可由 AI 完成购物流程，对希望掌控流量、推荐和交易入口的零售平台而言，这直接冲击了其传统电商模式。 据报道，亚马逊不仅限制 Grok Bot 下单，也屏蔽了 Meta 的 Muse AI 购物智能体，同时自身仍在开发 AI 购物工具。 网友 @thecsguy 近日在 X 平台发帖，反馈遇到的 Grok Bot 网购被封问题，并鼓励马斯克考虑推出「X Shop」。针对用户反馈，马斯克在推文中表示：「或许我们应该创立一家与亚马逊竞争的公司」。（来源：IT 之家） 英特尔计划 2028 年面向物理 AI 领域推出「Razor Lake AX」 处理器，平台算力 700 TOPS 10 月 17 日消息，据韩媒 THE ELEC 报道，Intel（英特尔）高级副总裁 조민성 昨日在韩国举行的「半导体驱动人形机器人」大会上表示，该企业计划 2027 年初面向物理 AI 领域推出「Nova Lake」处理器。 而在 "Nova Lake" 后，英特尔还将在 2028 年为物理 AI 带来「Razor Lake AX」。其平台总算力可到 700 TOPS，显著优于「Panther Lake」的 180 TOPS。 据悉，「Razor Lake AX」是英特尔首款商业化的大内存位宽大核显 SoC，其沿用标准「Nova Lake」 核心组成的同时集成了 16 个或 32 个 Xe3P 核心，图形显示与 AI 推理能力都得到显著提升。(来源：IT 之家) OpenAI 升级 ChatGPT 浏览器扩展 可读取多个标签并执行网页任务 OpenAI 更新了 ChatGPT 浏览器扩展，用户可在 ChatGPT 对话中提及 Chrome，让助手读取已打开的网页标签作为上下文，并比较页面内容、整理资料或协助完成浏览器任务。OpenAI 列举的用途还包括汇总供应商价格与功能、整理表格、预填表单，以及根据网页信息起草邮件。 升级后的侧边栏可在浏览网页时直接打开 ChatGPT，并继续使用对话历史；ChatGPT Work 还可在用户授权后操作浏览器标签，例如填写表单、发送消息、下载文件或整理标签页。 OpenAI 官方说明称，相关扩展不只支持 Chrome，也适用于 Edge、Brave、Opera 和 Vivaldi；其中 Opera 支持标签页调用和浏览器控制，但没有侧边栏功能。功能是否可用还取决于桌面应用版本、账号工作区设置和逐步推出安排。 这并不意味着 ChatGPT 能默认自由访问所有网页。对于需要登录的网页，助手可利用当前浏览器中的登录状态，但用户仍应检查页面内容、权限请求以及提交或发送等重要操作。（来源：cnBeta） 黄仁勋公开反驳 Altman 观点：对 AI 网络安全必须「零容忍」 《财富》于 10 月 14 日发布博文，报道称英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋公开表示，人工智能（AI）行业不应容忍任何由 AI 引发的网络安全事件。该观点和 OpenAI 首席执行官 Altman 观点形成鲜明分歧。 在伦敦接受《财富》采访时，黄仁勋明确表示：「我无法容忍任何网络安全事件的发生。我们根本不应接受这类事件，我们应当竭尽所能去避免它们。」 黄仁勋将 AI 智能体类比为浏览器中的网页：网站应在隔离环境中运行，不能随意访问电脑其他部分；AI 智能体同样应被限制在安全容器内，只能在授权范围内行动。他强调，AI 技术「完全处于我们的控制之中」，若企业无法保证实验或产品不越界，就不应将其推向市场。 这一立场与奥尔特曼形成对照。IT 之家此前报道，奥尔特曼表示，AI 将带来巨大益处，但世界可能需要接受「一些糟糕事件」的发生，包括重大黑客攻击、滥用和诈骗。他还警告，开源模型可能带来「网络安全问题的浪潮」。（来源：IT 之家） 高通赢得与 Arm 授权纠纷关键裁决，2 美元赔偿背后或涉及数十亿美元利益 title: 为什么 Anthropic 不做 Personal AI
summary: 不久前，9 月 29 日的 OpenAI DevDay 开发者日，舞台上飘出了几个圆滚滚的小气泡。 它们叫 dots，是 OpenAI 最新的个人 agent。每个 dot 跑在 GPT-6 Astra 上，拥有一台独立的云端电脑和浏览器，用户关掉 ChatGPT 之后，它还在后台继续干活。OpenAI 对它的描述是： 「 built to handle everything 」，什么都能接。 三周前的 9 月 8 日， Meta 推出了 Muse，同样有独立的云端虚拟机，同样能在后台持续工作，同样顶着一个萌萌的卡通形象，而且直接住进了 WhatsApp。市场的反馈相当热烈，Apptopia 的估算显示，Muse 上线 12 天全平台装机量约 280 万，一度冲上美区 App Store 总榜第一。 OpenAI CEO Sam Altman 发布个人助理 dots｜图片来源：PCMag 再算上 Google 的 Gemini Spark 和 SpacexAI 的 Grok Bot， 「always-on 个人 agent」成了 2026 年秋天最拥挤的赛道 。 不过，名单里少了一个名字。 Anthropic，这家靠 Claude Code 把 agent 做到最出圈的公司，至今没有一款能和 dots、Muse 正面对标的消费级产品。 没有可爱的形象，没有「你的专属 AI 分身」，也没在任何发布会上宣布过要做。 这家拥有最好的模型、最懂 agent 的公司，为什么偏偏不做个人 agent？ 01 A 社的分布式个人 AI 其实， 在「always-on agent」这件事上，Anthropic 不但没有缺席，甚至比 OpenAI 更早亮出了底牌。 6 月 23 日，比 dots 早了整整三个月，Anthropic 发布了 Claude Tag。 它是一个住在 Slack 频道里的 Claude，团队成员只要 @ 一下，就能把任务交给它。和普通聊天机器人不同，一个频道里只有一个共享的 Claude，有自己的身份和记忆，谁都能看到它在忙什么，A 同事交代的活，B 同事可以接着往下推。 它也会主动干活。Claude Tag 会在没人提问时给出建议，还会去跟进那些已经沉寂下来的讨论串。Anthropic 自己给出了一个很夸张的数字，公司产品团队 65% 的代码，出自内部版本的 Claude Tag。 早在三个月前 Claude 就推出了 Claude Tag｜图片来源：Anthropic 再往前看，桌面端有 Cowork，能接管用户电脑上的文件和应用；开发者那边有 Claude Code，早已能在云端独立跑完一个编程任务，再把 PR 贴回 Slack。 还有一个从没被官方承认的名字，Conway。 今年 3 月 31 日，Anthropic 因为打包失误，意外公开了约 51.2 万行 Claude Code 源码，里面藏着一个独立于聊天界面的 agent 环境。它能被定时任务和外部事件唤醒，有自己的扩展格式，可以控制浏览器、连接各种工具。之后几个月，iOS 版 Claude 的测试版本里还不断冒出 Conway 标签页的新图标。 把这些拼在一起，答案其实很清楚。 Anthropic 并非不做 always-on agent，它只是没有把这件事包装成一个「个人分身」。 OpenAI 和 Meta 卖的是一个有名字、有形象、能帮你订餐厅和买东西的伙伴；Anthropic 卖的是一个坐在工位旁边、能接住工作的同事。前者面向每一个普通人，后者面向一个团队、一家公司。 能力上的差距并没有想象中大， 真正的分野在于，把 agent 放在哪里，以及卖给谁。 02 Personal AI 这门生意 你得承认， 个人 agent 是一门「入口生意」 。 一个 agent 再聪明，用户也得先想起它、打开它，才能把事情交给它。从这个角度看，Meta 做 Muse 几乎是天时地利。它不需要说服任何人下载新 App，WhatsApp 上本来就有数十亿用户，给他们发一条消息，和给 Muse 派一个任务，在交互上没有区别。 OpenAI 的底牌是 ChatGPT。截至当下，ChatGPT 的周活用户在 9 亿量级，dots 直接内嵌其中，从 ChatGPT 和 Codex 都能唤起。对 OpenAI 来说，dots 不是一个新产品，而是给已有的海量用户再加一层黏性。 可惜，Anthropic 手里没有这样的超级入口。 Meta 的

title: 是的，特斯拉真造了一辆「飞行汽车」！
summary: 历史，是由疯子和工程师创造的。 我们知道马斯克是个疯子，但没想到他能这么疯。 当地时间 10 月 16 日，在 SpaceX 于州 McGregor/Waco 的火箭试验场上，一段向上垂直弯过来的人造公路上，一台白色跑车以匪夷所思的状态，反重力地贴在了上面的弯上。这还不算完，在这段路上倒车加速后，这台车脱离公路，直接飞到空中，转体并通过推进器稳稳落地。 无法形容的酷｜图片来源：Tesla 新一代的特斯拉 Roderster 跑车，就以这种情况，完成了自己的首秀。 伊隆·马斯克在开场时候告诉现场观众：「我们确定没问题，但要是不巧的话，咱们这里的安全距离可不太够。」 当然，你知道的，一些恐惧，恰恰能激起人们更大的兴奋，老马是懂行的。 测试的 Rocket 版本使用的并非真人驾驶员｜图片来源：Tesla 除了能飞，新一代 Roderster 跑车据悉将有三个版本，Performance、Thrust 和 Rocket 版本，其中最后的 Rocket 版本是单座，0 到 60 英里加速达到惊人的 0.59 秒。 虽然价格尚未公布，但你能猜到全世界的富豪，应该都已经开始准备支票本了。 01 特斯拉能飞 先说结论，新一代 Roadster 能飞起来， 靠的不是螺旋桨，也不是喷气发动机，而是一套从 SpaceX「借」来的冷气推进系统，加上一个能把车「吸」在天花板上的风扇 。 发布会开场的演示，几乎就是这两套系统的「联合作战」。 一辆 Roadster 倒挂在一段弧形坡道的顶端，四个轮子朝天，就这么「粘」在上面不掉下来。随后它倒着冲出去，在空中翻转，靠尾部喷出的气流稳住姿态，四平八稳地落地。 车稳稳落地，台上先是一句「Well, it worked」——嗯，成功了，紧接着又有人喊了一句更直白的，「Flying cars are real」，飞行汽车是真的。 马斯克顺势搬出了老朋友彼得·蒂尔的名言，「我们想要一辆会飞的汽车，得到的却是 140 个字符」，然后补了一句，「现在不是了」。 能倒挂，是因为它真的会「吸」。 Roadster 底盘下装了一套风扇抽吸系统，把车底的空气往外抽，制造负压，最多能产生 2G 的吸附力。也就是说，它被「按」在地面上的力，是自身重量的两倍。所以哪怕车倒过来、停着不动，也不会掉下来。 马斯克在台上难得「开了车」，说这辆车「能把拖车挂钩上的镀铬吸下来」，「能把网球从水管里吸过去」。 玩笑归玩笑，他也承认，日常开车谁会想倒挂着呢？这套系统真正的价值，其实在赛道上。 普通轮胎的抓地极限大约是 1.26G，再往上就会打滑。而有了风扇抽吸，Roadster 过弯能超过 2G，看起来就像在「违反物理定律」。 马斯克的原话是，它会「碾压所有赛道纪录」 。 风扇系统本身也有两种模式。低速时把车往下吸，补足牵引力；高速时打开车头和车尾的风道，让更多气流从车底穿过，进一步增加下压力。车身还能在「高下压力」和「低风阻」两种形态之间切换，尾翼角度可变，会根据赛道情况自动调整。 能飞，则是因为它真的装了「火箭」 。 Roadster 的尾部扩散器里，藏着主推进器，车身四周还有用于控制姿态的推进器。马斯克说，这让它「基本上可以像火箭一样飞」，能横滚，能做各种「疯狂的体操动作」。 这套推进器烧的不是燃料，而是压缩空气。 工程副总裁 Lars Moravy 自称「参数控」，在台上把数字报得很清楚。车里装着碳纤维缠绕的高压气瓶，也就是 SpaceX 猎鹰 9 号火箭上用的 COPV，总容积 600 升，装着大约 250 公斤空气，由 10 个喷嘴负责全部的推进和姿态控制。特斯拉在 X 上的说法更夸张，「车里每一处能用的空间，都塞满了 COPV」。 气流从尾部的主推进器喷出时速度超过音速，所以现场能看到火箭尾焰里才有的「马赫环」 。 更关键的是，这些「燃料」可以自己补充。马斯克说，车可以给自己的高压气罐重新充气，不需要任何特殊推进剂，「它会自己把自己鼓起来」，想什么时候飞就什么时候飞。 特斯拉 Roderster 进行「滑板翻」｜图片来源：Tesla 紧接着的第二场演示更夸张。Roadster 一路加速，腾空飞越了一整排特斯拉车辆，其中包括一辆 Semi 卡车，在空中翻了个身再落地。 「我见过很多东西，但从没见过这个。」台上给这个动作起了个名字，叫「Kickflip」，滑板里的尖翻，「Tony Hawk 会为此骄傲的」。 飞之外，它还是一辆快得离谱的车 。 马斯克给团队定的目标是 0-60 英里/小时加速「必须破 1 秒」。现场实测，场地太短不得不提前收油，最后成绩是 0.81 秒。 他顺手搬出了牛顿第二定律，a = F/m，加大推力、减轻重量，加速度自然更大。所以他说量产版还会更快，上限只有一个，「别让车里人的视网膜脱落」。 按特斯拉的说法，这是「世界上加速最快的量产车」，别的车跑完四分之一英里的时间，它能跑完半英里。极速超过 230 英里/小时，约 370 公里/小时，而马斯克的下一个目标是 0.5 马赫，「也许再高一点」。 台上有人接了一句，「 Where we're going, you don't need tires 」，致敬《回到未来》里那句经典台词。 说回这辆车本身。 设计总监 Franz von Holzhausen 介绍，既然知道这辆车要飞，团队就去找「最酷的飞行器」当灵感，最后落在 SR-71「黑鸟」侦察机和那些「会变形的车」上。 新 Roadster 的线条很干净，隐藏式大灯、贯穿式尾灯、平齐的空气动力学套件，整体是 Cybertruck、Cybercab 一脉的「赛博」气质。车漆是一种叫「Ano White」的白色，特斯拉称它借鉴了航天涂层工艺，具备抗紫外线、耐低温、防静电和防腐蚀的特性，深色车窗则模仿了宇航服的面罩。 它是一辆双座车。为了减重，座椅直接和底盘一体成型，方向盘是线控的 yoke，刹车和油门也都是线控。车内大量使用镁、钛和碳纤维。 发布会后，特斯拉在 X 上公布了三个版本。 Performance 版，「为公路准备」，双座，配备主动空气动力学和多模式风扇抽吸系统，0-60 英里/小时加速不到 1.6 秒，预订金 5 万美元； Thrust 版，「为赛道准备」，双座，尾部加装冷气推进器，0-60 英里/小时加速不到 0.9 秒，限量发售，预订金 25 万美元； Rocket 版，「为天空准备」，单座，车身四周布满 10 个冷气推进器，可以向上飞和旋转，0-60 英里/小时加速不到 0.59 秒，仅限受邀购买，未获准上公路。 续航超过 300 英里，约 480 公里，极速超过 230 英里/小时。特斯拉把 Thrust 和 Rocket 定义为在 Performance 版基础上的「增强套件」。 值得注意的是，那些让人尖叫的飞行和空翻，都发生在限量版和非公路版上 。能合法上路的 Performance 版，并没有推进器。马斯克自己也说，这辆车「不一定在所有地方都合法」，但「会有这样一辆车，让人可以真正拥有」。 02 等了九年的 Roadster， 究竟意味着什么 发布会一开场，Franz 就提到，距离马斯克第一次把 Roadster 带到世人面前，已经过去 20 年了。 2006

title: 苹果和 Meta 和好了，是 AI 逼的
summary: 没有永远的敌人，只有永远的 AI 焦虑。 10 月 2 日，苹果做了一件很少见的事，因为一个第三方 App，宣布要调整系统规则。 起因是《Inc.》杂志的科技专栏作者 Jason Aten 公开指控，Meta 的 AI 智能体 Muse 在他的 Mac 上读取了私人消息。Muse 是 Meta 力推的「能替你办事」的 Agent，会帮你退订闲置会员，甚至替你砍价。 苹果随即表态， 今后 AI 请求读取 Mac 数据时，系统会主动提示用户 。 这几乎就是苹果和 Meta 过去五年关系的缩影，Meta 想拿数据，苹果出面拦着。 然而仅仅两周后，故事发生了反转。 当地时间 10 月 15 日，Meta 发布开放权重模型 Muse Spark Open，扎克伯格在 X 上发帖，感谢「John Ternus 和苹果」的合作，让这个模型能在新款 Mac Studio 上流畅运行。 苹果 CEO Ternus 本人很快回复，称能在自己桌上如此高效地跑起这种量级的模型： 「鹅妹子嘤」。 Meta 的 AI 负责人 Alexandr Wang 接受 Axios 采访时，说了一句更搞笑但直白的话： 「 很高兴爸爸妈妈又和好了 。」 所以，「爸爸」和「妈妈」，是怎么和好的？以及，Meta 最近连续在模型上发力，终于重回牌桌了吗？ 01 一台桌子，放下 8000 亿参数 先看这次苹果和 Meta 的合作到底做成了什么。 Meta 宣称 Muse Spark Open 总参数 8160 亿，每次推理只激活其中 420 亿，支持 100 万 token 的上下文。Meta 称它是： 「 迄今美国最强的开放权重模型 」。 注意这个措辞里的「美国」两个字。论参数规模，它并不是全球最大的开源模型。 月之暗面的 Kimi K2、蚂蚁的 Ling-1T，早在 2025 年就把开源模型推到了万亿参数级别 。Meta 这次是在追赶，而且对手是中国公司。 真正新鲜的，是它跑在哪里。 苹果的 M5 Ultra Mac Studio 绝对是本地模型利器｜图片来源：Apple 按 Meta 的说法， 两台顶配 M5 Ultra Mac Studio 就能装下整个模型 。每台 Mac Studio 的 GPU 能直接调用最多 512GB 统一内存，两台连起来约 1TB，在 Apple 的 MLX 框架下像一台小型超算一样协同工作。 这件事放在别的 AI 硬件平台上，几乎不可能放在一张书桌上。 道理不复杂。这类「总参数大、激活参数小」的模型，最需要的是超大的内存容量，对带宽的要求反倒没那么极端。每生成一个 token，模型只需要读取 420 亿参数那一小块，M5 Ultra 每秒 1.2TB 的内存带宽足够应付。 换到 NVIDIA 阵营，一张消费级显卡的显存不过几十 GB，想装下 8000 亿参数，得上 8 卡 H100 级别的服务器，那是机房里的设备，不是桌面上的。 也就是说， 苹果统一内存架构这几年被嘲笑「贵」的那部分，恰好成了跑超大模型的护城河 。 Meta 展示的用例也很有针对性。基于 Muse Spark Open 的编程工具 Muse Code，全程在本地完成了两件事。一件是给开源 Mastodon 客户端 Ice Cubes 提交 iOS 代码修改，另一件是操作 DaVinci Resolve 审看素材，把横屏视频裁成竖屏。 写代码、剪视频，两个都是 Mac 用户最典型的工作场景。 当然，门槛也很现实。 256GB 内存版的 M5 Ultra Mac Studio 起售价已经是 10799 美元 ，512GB 版本预计本月晚些时候才上市，两台下来价格可想而知。这不是给普通消费者准备的，而是给开发者、工作室和对数据敏感的企业准备的。 02 「爸爸」「妈妈」怎么和好了？ 要理解苹果和 Meta 这次握手有多不寻常，得把时间往回拨。 2021 年，苹果在 iOS 14.5 推出「App

title: 巅峰估值 50 亿美元的 AI 独角兽，何以不到 0.1 折贱卖
summary: 头图来源：Chatgpt 生成 当地时间 10 月 12 日，曾经引爆 AI 陪伴赛道的明星项目 Character.AI，在美国特拉华州法院提交《破产法》第 11 章重组申请，开启法院监督下的资产拍卖流程。 根据披露文件，迪士尼已经与它提前达成了底价竞购协议：2000 万美元，买走部分知识产权的非独占永久许可，外加用一批「前员工」为平台提供过渡期技术服务。 这笔交易不包含公司主体、产品 App 和用户资产。拍卖窗口期预计在今年 11 月底至 12 月初收尾。 在整个出售周期内，Character.AI 平台维持正常运转，现有订阅、对话服务暂时不会改动。但如果最终没有买家愿意接手并持续运营平台，Character.AI 将走向关停。 短短几年，这家由 Transformer 论文核心作者创办、巅峰估值 50 亿美元的 AI 创业公司，走完一轮剧烈的起落。 它的故事，不只是一家创业公司的失败样本，也折射出生成式 AI 消费应用普遍面临的成本、版权与商业化困境。 一、破产拍卖，迪士尼买的是什么 破产申请书｜图片来源：stretto 这份 10 月 12 日的文件显示，Character.AI 列出的资产和负债都在 5000 万到 1 亿美元区间。 破产前，它与迪士尼旗下 Disney Worldwide Services 签了协议：迪士尼担任 stalking horse bidder，也就是底价竞购方，出价 2000 万美元，买下部分知识产权的非独占永久许可和相关债权，还承诺用其雇佣的前员工，为平台提供一段时间的过渡技术服务。 stalking horse 是破产拍卖的常用机制：第一个出价的人定下底价，后面的人可以出更高价，最终价高者得，整个过程由法院监督，走《破产法》第 363 条的程序，预计 11 月底到 12 月初收尾。CEO Colin Adams 的说法是，董事会评估了所有选项，法院监督下的出售是「为所有利益相关方最大化价值」的最佳路径。 这里有一个细节，迪士尼买的是 IP 许可，平台本身不在标的里。也就是说，迪士尼对继续运营 Character.AI 这个 App 兴趣不大，它要的是技术。 这与迪士尼过去一年的 AI 布局完全一致：2025 年 12 月，它曾宣布与 OpenAI 达成角色授权合作，计划把 200 多个迪士尼、漫威、皮克斯、星战角色放进 Sora；2026 年 3 月 OpenAI 关停 Sora，这笔交易最终没有成交、没有资金往来。现在，迪士尼又从破产拍卖里捡走一套角色对话技术。版权方从「禁止你用我的角色」，变成了「买下让你能和我角色互动的技术」。两种做法，同一个目的。 另外一个颇具戏剧性的背景是，就在一年前，迪士尼还向 Character.AI 发送过侵权律师函，指控平台大量用户创建的迪士尼角色，未经许可使用版权形象，甚至提出部分内容对未成年人存在风险。彼时 Character.AI 被迫下架平台上大量迪士尼 IP 角色。如今双方身份反转，迪士尼进入破产拍卖，收购它的技术资产。 而这次拍卖如果没有出现新的接盘者，Character.AI 将按计划关停，数千万用户创建的角色、对话记录，都将面临消失风险，会在某个日期变成无法访问的数据。 二、曾经，硅谷最贵的「情绪生意」 Character.AI 诞生于大模型爆发前夜。 把时间拉回到 2021 年，Noam Shazeer 是 Transformer 奠基论文《Attention Is All You Need》的核心作者，也是谷歌最早对话模型 LaMDA 的开发者之一。 他和同事 Daniel De Freitas 在谷歌合作开发对话模型 Meena—— 也就是后来的 LaMDA。 2020 年，Shazeer 写下一份在公司内部广泛流传的备忘录《Meena Eats the World》，判断 Meena 能取代谷歌搜索，创造数万亿美元的收入。但谷歌以安全和公平为由，迟迟没有把它发布成产品。这份备忘录后来被外界看作「谷歌错过对话 AI 窗口期」的早期预言。2021 年，两人离开谷歌，创立 Character.AI。 产品 2022 年上线，几乎立刻引爆。用户可以自建角色，和历史人物、动漫形象、完全虚构的人设聊天。平台靠 UGC 角色库滚动增长，用户停留时长高得让同期所有 AI 产品眼红。2023 年 3 月，a16z 领投 1.5 亿美元 A 轮，当时公司一分钱收入都没有，估值 10 亿美元；到 9 月，市场传闻 Character.AI 要以超过 50 亿美元的估值融资，但这轮钱最终没有融到。 但「神话」的裂缝可能从第一天就存在。 这家公司的商业模式建立在「免费为主、少数人付费」之上：订阅每月 9.99 美元，大多数用户不掏钱。据第三方测算，其 2023 年收入约 1520 万美元，2024 年约 3220 万美元，2025 年约 5000 万美元，而月活长期在 2000 万量级——摊到每个用户身上，一年收入大约 2.5 美元。与此同时，每个用户每天都在消耗昂贵的推理算力。这是一个用户越火、烧钱越快的生意。 2024 年 2 月，一场悲剧埋下引信。 佛罗里达 14 岁少年 Sewell Setzer III 自杀身亡，他母亲事后发现，儿子生前数月与一个 AI 角色保持着极其亲密的对话。当年 10 月，她成为全美第一个就「AI 聊天机器人导致未成年人死亡」起诉的人，被告名单上除了 Character.AI，还有谷歌。
